name: Cross-race effect
statement: People recognise faces of their own race more accurately than faces of another race, scoring more hits, fewer false alarms and better discrimination.
meaning: The claim is about recognition memory rather than attitude. A participant studies a set of faces, then sees those faces mixed with new ones and says which are old. Own-race faces produce more correct hits and fewer false alarms than other-race faces, a pattern the literature calls a mirror effect. Because both measures move, the difference shows up in signal-detection terms as sensitivity, not only as willingness to say old. That distinction is why Singh and colleagues prefer the label cross-race recognition deficit, following Levin: own-race bias names it as a response bias, which is not what the data show. The effect is studied because of eyewitness identification, and the two measures are not the same thing. The laboratory scores hits and false alarms against a studied list. A lineup asks a witness to pick one person, or nobody, from a set built by police, and the field record does not carry the laboratory result cleanly.

origin.who: Roy S. Malpass and Jerome Kravitz
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Malpass and Kravitz's 'Recognition for faces of own and other race' is the paper the field cites as its starting point. The article could not be obtained at Unpaywall, Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, PubMed or general web search, and the PubMed record carries no abstract, so nothing on this page rests on its contents. Crossref and OpenAlex both give the second author's forename as Jerome; PubMed records only the initial. The modern evidence base dates from Meissner and Brigham's 2001 meta-analysis in Psychology, Public Policy, and Law, which gave the effect its standing in law as well as in psychology.

evidence: The largest count of the literature is Lee and Penrod's three-level meta-analysis. It took in 159 journal articles published between 1969 and 2021 and 747 effect sizes: 205 for hit rates, 125 for false alarm rates, 261 for discriminability and 158 for response criterion. Across within-subject designs the pooled Hedges' g for discriminability was 0.54, 95% CI [0.49, 0.60]. Hits favoured own-race faces at g = 0.30 [0.22, 0.38], and response criterion came out at g = 0.30 [0.21, 0.39], with own-race faces judged against a stricter standard. The six between-subject effect sizes for discriminability gave a smaller and looser estimate, g = 0.36 [0.06, 0.66], and the seven for false alarms gave g = -0.22 [-0.39, -0.05]. No pooled within-subject figure for false alarms appears here. The authors' OSF project posts forest plots for six of the eight measure-by-design cells, and the two it omits are hit rates between subjects and false alarms within subjects, so that estimate could not be read. Splitting by design rather than by measure, the authors report pooled Hedges' gav for two-way designs of 0.37 for hits, -0.46 for false alarms, 0.51 for discriminability and 0.14 for criterion, on 88, 52, 129 and 74 effect sizes; for one-way designs the figures are 0.26, -0.61, 0.57 and 0.40, on 117, 73, 132 and 84. Participant race, white against non-white, and the interval between study and test were the two moderators that held up. Meissner and Brigham's 2001 meta-analysis analysed 39 research articles, 91 independent samples and nearly 5,000 participants, examined eight moderators, and reported the mirror pattern together with an own-race bias in aggregate measures of discrimination accuracy and response criterion. That is its abstract, read at OpenAlex. Its own pooled figures could not be read, because the article is closed access and the repository copy listed at the University of Texas at El Paso returned 403 on every attempt.

replication.headline: The recognition-memory finding is one of the sturdier results in the field: a meta-analysis of 159 articles spanning 1969 to 2021 puts the own-race advantage in discrimination at Hedges' g = 0.54, 95% CI [0.49, 0.60].
replication.detail: Lee and Penrod report that sensitivity analysis and publication-bias analysis both supported the robustness of the effect, and that it replicated the earlier meta-analyses despite decades of rising diversity. The pooled estimates move in the directions the mirror-effect account predicts and none of the intervals crosses zero. Direction is not the same as explanation, and the contact account is where the evidence thins. Singh, Mellinger, Earls, Tran, Bardsley and Correll gathered 207 statistical tests from 96 independent samples in 65 papers and found that more cross-race contact went with a smaller deficit at r = -.148, 95% CI [-.198, -.096]. That is 2.18% of the variation in the deficit. Meissner and Brigham's estimate, as Singh and colleagues describe it, was r = -.13 from 29 studies, or about 1.7%. The funnel plot was asymmetric, trim and fill estimated 26 missing samples, and the adjusted estimate fell to r = -.050 [-.082, -.018]. Published samples gave r = -.174 [-.229, -.116] and unpublished ones r = -.056 [-.162, .052], which did not clear zero, and the gap between the two was marginal: rdiff = -.119, 95% CI [-.237, .003], p = .056. Manipulated contact was the strongest operationalisation at r = -.382 [-.561, -.170], which the authors put at 14.61% of the variation. The Social Experience Questionnaire was the one operationalisation whose interval crossed zero, r = -.076 [-.196, .046], p = .219. Contact reported for childhood was stronger than contact reported for adulthood: r = -.335 before age six, -.253 for ages six to twelve, -.257 for ages twelve to eighteen, -.128 after eighteen and -.124 for lifetime contact. Adult contact still had an interval clear of zero. Singh and colleagues found no evidence that the contact relationship depended on participant race, F(3, 203) = 1.373, p = .252. Meissner and Brigham had found the contact relationship growing stronger over time; in the larger dataset it grew weaker.

study.cite: Lee, J., & Penrod, S. D. (2022). Three-level meta-analysis of the other-race bias in facial identification. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 36(5), 1106-1130.

limits: Nobody has shown what causes the effect. Perceptual expertise, category-focused attention and motivation are the three standing accounts, and the tests that would separate them keep coming back null. Singh and colleagues found no evidence that the nature of face processing moderated the contact relationship, F(2, 204) = 1.85, p = .161, which is what Hancock and Rhodes' configural account predicts a difference in. Cruz, Palma, Bansemer, Correll, Fonseca, Gonçalves and Santos ran a registered replication of the individuation instructions that Hugenberg, Miller and Claypool reported as reducing the effect. They recruited 520 white participants in the United States and 361 in Portugal, analysing 310 and 293. Individuation instructions did not reduce the effect in either country, and Bayesian analysis favoured its absence. Contact is the best-supported influence and it is small, contested in shape, and possibly age-bounded. McKone and seven colleagues tested 373 people in Australia across four samples, using race-specific and ethnicity-specific versions of the Cambridge Face Memory Test, so their measure pools an other-race with an other-ethnicity effect. Contact in primary school predicted a smaller effect in all 20 correlations, thirteen of them reliable at p < 0.05 uncorrected, on the smaller n of 57 that met their range criterion. Secondary-school contact reached p = 0.063 across N = 223 and adult contact p = 0.119, on correlations run at N = 120. Singh's meta-analysis found adult contact did work, and tested the before-twelve window directly: the pattern trended in the predicted direction and was not clearly supported, rdiff = -.213, 95% CI [-.452, .055], p = .118. Wong, Stephen and Keeble tested 94 people in Malaysia and found the effect in Malay, Chinese and Western Caucasian participants but not prominently in Indian participants, and no relationship between self-reported interracial contact and its size. Their second experiment, which restored hair and facial contour, abolished the effect. Töredi, Mansour, Jones, Skelton and McIntyre argue from the articles in the recent meta-analyses that minority-race status may explain why many studies of non-white participants find no effect, and that the literature's concentration on majority-race participants viewing minority-race faces makes the effect look more general than it is. The search ran across Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Europe PMC, PubMed, Semantic Scholar, OSF, the Psychological Science Accelerator site and the open web, and found no multi-laboratory preregistered replication of the basic effect. The registered replication that exists tested an intervention. Meissner and Brigham's 2001 article was not read; only its abstract was. Sporer's companion review in the same issue is closed access and was not read. Lee and Penrod's article is also paywalled: the pooled estimates above were read off the forest plots and Supplemental Table 5 on OSF, not off the article. Almost all of this work is laboratory recognition memory, and the entry says nothing about facial-recognition software or about children.
misreadings: The contact hypothesis is treated as the explanation, and the number it rests on is 2.18% of variance. Contact matters and it does not carry the effect, and the trim-and-fill estimate of r = -.050 suggests even that share may be inflated by what went unpublished. The effect is read as prejudice. It is a difference in discrimination accuracy, and no measure of attitude is required to produce it. It is also read as universal, and that is the claim the recent work presses on. Lee and Penrod found participant race, white against non-white, to be one of only two stable moderators. Marsh, Reisberg, Pezdek and Shao, testing black and white participants on faces repeated across five blocks, report the pattern plainly evident in white participants and not in black ones, with false alarms and d' showing it across all five blocks and hit rates showing none of it. Calling it own-race bias invites a third error, because the criterion shift and the sensitivity difference are separate findings and only the second is what the phrase 'they all look alike' is usually pointing at. The Innocence Project's figure is the most misquoted. Of 375 DNA exonerations between 1989 and 2020, 69% involved an eyewitness misidentification, and 42% of those misidentifications were cross-racial. That is a share of known wrongful convictions, not a rate at which cross-racial identifications go wrong, and the denominator that would make it one does not exist. Field data are thinner than the laboratory would suggest. Valentine, Pickering and Darling analysed 640 identification attempts across 314 real lineups run by the Metropolitan Police in London and found no independent, statistically reliable effect of cross-race identification, alongside no reliable effect of weapon focus or delay. Their abstract does report that suspects were more likely to be identified when white European rather than African-Caribbean.

sources.text: Malpass, R. S., & Kravitz, J. (1969). Recognition for faces of own and other race. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 13(4), 330-334. The founding citation. Listed because it exists; the article could not be obtained at Unpaywall, Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, PubMed or web search, and the PubMed record has no abstract, so no claim here comes from it.

Meissner, C. A., & Brigham, J. C. (2001). Thirty years of investigating the own-race bias in memory for faces: A meta-analytic review. Psychology, Public Policy, and Law, 7(1), 3-35. Abstract read in full at OpenAlex and the source for the 39 articles, 91 samples, nearly 5,000 participants and eight moderators. The article itself is closed access; the repository copy listed at the University of Texas at El Paso returned 403, so its pooled figures and odds ratios are not on this page.

Sporer, S. L. (2001). Recognizing faces of other ethnic groups: An integration of theories. Psychology, Public Policy, and Law, 7(1), 36-97. The companion review in the same issue. Metadata verified at Crossref, which carries no abstract; Unpaywall records no open copy. Not read; no claim here comes from it.

Lee, J., & Penrod, S. D. (2022). Three-level meta-analysis of the other-race bias in facial identification. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 36(5), 1106-1130. Abstract read in full at Crossref and the source for the 159 articles, the years 1969 to 2021 and the two surviving moderators.

Lee, J., & Penrod, S. D. (2022). Three-level meta-analysis of the other-race bias in facial identification: supplemental materials and raw data. OSF project sj2tg. Source for the pooled Hedges' g values, their intervals and the counts of effect sizes. Six forest plots are posted and two are not.

Singh, B., Mellinger, C., Earls, H. A., Tran, J., Bardsley, B., & Correll, J. (2022). Does cross-race contact improve cross-race face perception? A meta-analysis of the cross-race deficit and contact. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 48(6), 865-887. Read in full from the author manuscript at par.nsf.gov.

McKone, E., Wan, L., Pidcock, M., Crookes, K., Reynolds, K., Dawel, A., Kidd, E., & Fiorentini, C. (2019). A critical period for faces: Other-race face recognition is improved by childhood but not adult social contact. Scientific Reports, 9, 12820. Full text read from the publisher PDF.

Wong, H. K., Stephen, I. D., & Keeble, D. R. T. (2020). The own-race bias for face recognition in a multiracial society. Frontiers in Psychology, 11, 208. Full text read at Europe PMC and the source for the 94 participants, the weak result in Indian participants and the second experiment that abolished the effect.

Töredi, D., Mansour, J. K., Jones, S. E., Skelton, F., & McIntyre, A. (2025). The impact of minority-race status on the cross-race effect: A critical review. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 20(6), 1033-1048. Abstract read at Crossref and PubMed; the article is closed access and its body was not read.

Marsh, B. U., Reisberg, D., Pezdek, K., & Shao, T. (2025). Does the cross-race effect persist for repeatedly viewed faces? Memory, 33(10), 1253-1265. Abstract read at PubMed and Europe PMC and the source for the asymmetry between black and white participants and for the hit-rate null. Paywalled; the body was not read.

Hugenberg, K., Miller, J., & Claypool, H. M. (2007). Categorization and individuation in the cross-race recognition deficit: Toward a solution to an insidious problem. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 43(2), 334-340. The study the registered replication targeted; metadata verified at Crossref, which carries no abstract, and Unpaywall records no open copy. Text not read.

Cruz, F., Palma, T. A., Bansemer, E., Correll, J., Fonseca, S., Gonçalves, P., & Santos, A. S. (2023). Do individuation instructions reduce the cross-race effect? A registered replication of Hugenberg, Miller, and Claypool (2007). Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 104, 104423. Unpaywall lists an open copy at the University of Lisbon repository; that host refused every connection across five attempts, so the article was not read. The recruited and analysed sample sizes and the null result are taken from the authors' own report to the European Association of Social Psychology, linked here.

Valentine, T., Pickering, A., & Darling, S. (2003). Characteristics of eyewitness identification that predict the outcome of real lineups. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 17(8), 969-993. Abstract read at Crossref; the source for the field null on cross-race identification. The Wiley full text returned 403 and was not read.
Innocence Project. DNA exonerations in the United States (1989-2020). Source for the 375 exonerations, the 69% involving eyewitness misidentification and the 42% of those that were cross-racial.
